title: Biological Diversity Act 2002 and Benefit Sharing

cards.b:
The Biological Diversity Act is the Indian law that puts the Convention on Biological Diversity into practice. Prelims asks about its three-tier structure, the NBA, People's Biodiversity Registers and the 2023 amendment. Mains links it to biopiracy, traditional knowledge and tribal rights.

It is a short Act, so exact detail pays.

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 aims at conservation, sustainable use and fair sharing of benefits. It created a three-tier body system:

  • National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Chennai, set up in 2003. Statutory, autonomous.
  • State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) in states.
  • Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) at local-body level.

BMCs prepare People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs), which record local knowledge about species and uses.

• Foreign nationals, NRIs and foreign companies need NBA approval to access biological resources or knowledge in India.
  • Indian citizens and companies must give prior intimation to the State Board for commercial use.
  • Applying for an intellectual property right based on Indian material (for example a patent) needs NBA approval (Section 6).
  • Local communities and vaidyas and hakims are exempt from the approval rules for traditional use.

The NBA sets benefit-sharing terms, such as royalty or a share of fees.

Under Section 37, a state can notify areas of biodiversity importance as Biological Heritage Sites (BHS). The first was Nallur Tamarind Grove near Bengaluru (2007). Other examples include Ameenpur Lake in Telangana and Dhinodhar Hills in Gujarat.

The Act also lets the Centre notify threatened species and prohibit or regulate their collection. Sections 36 and 38 relate to such species.

BMCs may be consulted by the state and get benefit funds, under the Act's rules.

Parliament passed the amendment in July 2023. Main changes:

  • Decriminalised many offences, with penalties from Rs 1 lakh up to Rs 50 lakh instead of jail for several breaches.
  • Exempted AYUSH practitioners (codified traditional medicine) and some cultivated medicinal plants from benefit sharing requirements.
  • Required prior intimation from Indian users and gave BMCs a share in benefits.
  • Eased research, patents and bio-survey and use.

Critics fear a weakened regime for local communities.

Biopiracy is taking resources or knowledge without consent. India's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) holds documented formulae in several languages for patent examiners. The Act also ties in with patent rules: a patent for an invention based on Indian biological material must disclose its source in the application.

The Patents Act was amended in 2002 for this disclosure requirement.

Industry argues approvals slowed research and pharma, and sees the 2023 changes as modernising. Activists argue the Act's soul, community control over biological resources, was lost. Another issue is that many BMCs exist only on paper, and PBRs are incomplete.

A fair summary is that the Act has the right design but weak local capacity, since most BMCs lack funds and trained members.

A well-known case is the Kani tribe of Kerala and the drug Jeevani from the plant arogyapacha (*Trichopus zeylanicus*). The Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute licensed the formula, and the Kani Trust received a share of fees and royalties. It is cited as the best Indian ABS example (late 1990s).

Other cases: NBA action on neem and basmati disputes, and a case against firms that used Indian resources without approval.

• Act: 2002. NBA: 2003, Chennai.
  • Three tiers: NBA, SBB, BMC.
  • PBR: record kept by BMC.
  • Heritage Sites: Section 37; first Nallur Tamarind Grove, Bengaluru.
  • Amendment: 2023, decriminalisation and AYUSH exemption.
  • Parent treaty: CBD.

Remember the sequence: CBD 1992, Act 2002, NBA 2003, first Heritage Site 2007, Nagoya Protocol 2010, amendment 2023.

Prelims-style: "National Biodiversity Authority is located at" (Chennai). "BMCs prepare People's Biodiversity Registers."

Mains-style: "How effective is the Biological Diversity Act in preventing biopiracy and ensuring benefit sharing?" Structure: aims; institutions; ABS example (Kani); limits; 2023 amendment; way forward (empower BMCs, TKDL, funds).

Quote the Kani and Jeevani case as the model of fair benefit sharing in any ABS answer.
